The constants are exact, but the load-bearing mechanism — "still surfaces at 30% weight, so a wrong rejection is recoverable by a later query" — is refuted on three independent grounds, all checked against the source clone at /Users/seventyleven/Desktop/researchfms/hyperresearch/src/hyperresearch/ rather than the teardown.

(1) THE MULTIPLIER IS POST-LIMIT AND CANNOT AFFECT RETRIEVAL. search/fts.py runs `ORDER BY score LIMIT ? OFFSET ?` in SQL (:96-97) on the RAW BM25 score. Only after `fetchall()` does Python apply the status multipliers and re-sort (:128-140). Membership of the result set is decided entirely before the multiplier exists. Empirically confirmed on a copy of the researchfms vault (79 notes): marking the rank-10 hit `evergreen` (x1.5) did NOT pull it into a limit=5 result; marking the rank-21 hit `deprecated` changed nothing because it was never in the page. So the x0.3 supplies zero recovery mechanism. A deprecated note surfaces at all only because the default query applies no status filter — the claim mis-attributes that separate fact to the multiplier, and the multiplier's only actual effect is to guarantee the note ranks last in whatever page it already won.

(2) "30% WEIGHT" MISDESCRIBES THE EFFECT SIZE. Measured BM25 spread across the top-10 of a real query is 8.4% (1.1439 .. 1.0474). Against that distribution x0.3 is not a graded 30% demotion — it drops a hit to 0.343 against a field of ~1.13, i.e. dead last, every time, behind every non-deprecated result. 3. The paper already concedes the point the finding claims to have discovered, so there is nothing to expose: "the DepMap score is primarily meant to function as a sanity check and filter out obviously incorrect candidates but is unlikely to be predictive of efficacy." The gate was never advanced as an efficacy predictor, and nothing in the AML results tests its actual job (removing obviously wrong candidates).
